title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The Cid content with his sons-in-law; their boasting and the household's jests (tiradas 120–123, lines 2474–2542)
part: Tiradas 120–123 · The Cid content with his sons-in-law; their boasting and the household's jests (lines 2474–2542)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 284–288, lines 2474–2542 (tiradas 120–123). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t:
Grant f[o] el dia [por] la cort del Campeador,
después que esta batalla vencieron e al rey Búcar mató,
alçó la mano, a la barba se tomó:
sentences.l:
Great wa[s] the day [through] the court of-the Campeador,
after that this battle they-won and the king Búcar he-killed,
he-raised the hand, to the beard himself he-took:
sentences.i: Great was the day throughout the Campeador's court, after they had won this battle and he had killed King Búcar. He raised his hand and took hold of his beard:
sentences.n: Tirada 120 (assonance ó) — the Çid content with his victory and with his sons-in-law; a repetition (Pidal: El Cid satisfecho de su victoria y de sus yernos. (Repetición)). The line-ends run Campeador, mató, tomó, señor, sabor, dos, Carrión, pro: stressed ó. Pidal marks the tirada a repetition: it goes back over the matter of tirada 119 (the victory, the Çid's pleasure in his sons-in-law, the good news that will go to Carrión) in a new assonance, as the epic often tells a moment twice. f[o] = fue, 'was', the o Pidal's; [por], the whole word his. dia unaccented, as printed. Grant … el dia, a great day, a day of rejoicing. vencieron, plural, the whole host; mató, singular, the Çid, who killed Búcar at v. 2425. The hand raised and the beard grasped in 2476 are the Çid's too: the subject of mató runs on unnamed into alçó and se tomó. Taking hold of his beard is the Çid's gesture of satisfaction and pride; the beard is his honour.

sentences.t:
“Grado a Cristus, que del mundo es señor,
quando veo lo que avía sabor,
que lidiaran comigo en campo mios yernos amos a dos
sentences.l:
“Thanks to Christ, who of-the world is lord,
when I-see that which I-had desire-for,
that had-fought with-me in field my sons-in-law both two
sentences.i: “Thanks be to Christ, who is lord of the world, now that I see what I longed for: my two sons-in-law have fought beside me in the field.
sentences.n: Grado a Cristus, 'thanks to Christ', Cristus in its Latin form. avía = había, here first person, 'I had'; aver sabor (de), 'to have a liking, a longing (for)'. Pidal's note to v. 2478: 'cuando veo lo que [tanto] deseaba' — 'when I see what I [so much] desired'. lidiaran, the -ra form as a pluperfect, 'had fought'; comigo = conmigo. en campo, 'in the field', in pitched battle. amos a dos, 'both of the two'. The Çid believes it; the hearers have been told otherwise, of Fernando's flight from the Moor (the chronicle prose Pidal sets in the lost folio of tirada 115), and at v. 2464 the Infantes took this kind of praise as mockery. Pidal prints a raised dot after dos, perhaps a broken colon or semicolon, perhaps only a speck; the line is left unpunctuated here, and the reading is uncertain.

sentences.t:
mandados buenos irán dellos a Carrión,
commo son ondrados e aver [n]os [han] grant pro.”
sentences.l:
tidings good will-go of-them to Carrión,
how they-are honoured and have [u]s [they-will] great profit.”
sentences.i: Good tidings of them will go to Carrión: how they are held in honour, and how they will be of great profit to us.”
sentences.n: mandados, 'tidings, reports'; the Çid said almost the same at v. 2445 (a Carrión de vos irán buenos mandados). dellos = de ellos. ondrados, 'honoured', with ond- for hon-. aver [n]os [han], the split future of aver with the pronoun between (= nos avrán): 'they will have for us', with grant pro, 'great profit, advantage': the sons-in-law will be a gain to the house. Both the n of nos and the whole word han are Pidal's restorations; he gives no note, and the exact turn of the phrase is not certain.

sentences.t:
Sobejanas son las ganançias que todos an ganad[o];
lo uno es [dellos], lo otro han en salvo.
sentences.l:
Exceeding are the gains that all have gained;
the one is [theirs], the other they-have in safety.
sentences.i: Beyond all measure are the gains they have all won: part is their own already, the rest they hold in safe keeping.
sentences.n: Tirada 121 (assonance á-o) — the sharing of the booty (Pidal: Reparto del botín). The line-ends run ganad[o], salvo, nasco, arrancado, contado, olbidado, acordados, cavallos, largos, contados: stressed á, then o. Sobejanas, 'excessive, overflowing'. an = han; ganad[o], the o Pidal's. [dellos] = de ellos, 'theirs', the whole word his correction. Pidal's note to v. 2483: Verso difícil, que creo significa: 'lo uno es propiedad ya antigua de ellos; lo otro, de esta batalla, lo tienen ya a buen recaudo' — 'a difficult line, which I believe means: "the one is already their own property of old; the other, from this battle, they already have in safe keeping"'. He adds that Bertoni, accepting his correction dellos, takes it as 'una parte era stata divisa sul campo (ed erano a ciascuno toccati seicento marchi), l'altra parte fu posta in sicuro' — 'one part had been shared out on the field (and six hundred marks had fallen to each man), the other part was put in safety'; and that, believing the Çid's speech still runs on, Hinard translates 'une partie est nôtre, le reste leur appartient' ('one part is ours, the rest belongs to them') and Bello, más libremente, 'more freely', 'guardemos lo nuestro i cuidemos de la seguridad común' ('let us keep what is ours and look to the common safety'). The sense is uncertain. en salvo, 'in safety', as at v. 2469.

sentences.t:
Mandó mio Çid, el que en buen ora nasco,
desta batalla que han arrancado
que todos prisiessen so derecho contado,
e el so quinto [de mio Çid] non f[o]sse olbidado.
sentences.l:
Commanded my Çid, he who in good hour was-born,
of-this battle that they-have won
that all should-take their right reckoned,
and the his fifth [of my Çid] not should-b[e] forgotten.
sentences.i: My Çid, who was born in a good hour, gave order that from this battle they had won every man should take his due share, counted out, and that my Çid's own fifth should not be forgotten.
sentences.n: el que en buen ora nasco, the formula, 'he who was born in a good hour'; nasco, strong preterite of naçer. arrancar una batalla, 'to win a battle' (to rout the enemy). prisiessen, imperfect subjunctive of prender, 'should take'. so derecho contado, 'his right, counted out': each man's lawful share. el so quinto, article + possessive, 'his fifth': the lord's fifth of all booty, his by custom; [de mio Çid], the whole phrase Pidal's restoration. f[o]sse = fuesse, the o his. olbidado = olvidado, with b for v.

sentences.t: Assí lo fazen todos, ca eran acordados.
sentences.l: So it they-do all, for they-were prudent.
sentences.i: And so they all did, for they were men of sense.
sentences.n: fazen, present among pasts, with f- for modern h- (hacen). ca, 'for'. Pidal's note: acordados, 'prudentes', v. 1290 — 'prudent, sensible'.

sentences.t:
Ca[di]erónle en quinta al Çid seys çientos cavallos,
e otras azémilas e camellos largos
tantos son de muchos que non serién contados.
sentences.l:
Fell-to-him in fifth to-the Çid six hundred horses,
and other sumpter-mules and camels in-plenty
so-many they-are of many that not they-would-be counted.
sentences.i: Six hundred horses fell to the Çid as his fifth, and sumpter-mules besides, and camels in plenty; so very many were they that they could not be counted.
sentences.n: Ca[di]erónle = cadieron + le, 'fell to him', cadieron the old preterite of caer (= cayeron); al Çid names the le. The di is Pidal's restoration; the establishing run judged C-a roman, and the exact extent of the italic is not certain. en quinta, 'in (his) fifth'. seys çientos = seiscientos. azémilas, 'sumpter-mules, beasts of burden'. Pidal's note to v. 2490: camellos largos, 'camellos en abundancia'; compárese 804 — 'camels in abundance; compare v. 804'. Pidal's note to v. 2491: tantos son de muchos, 'tantísimos son' — 'they are so very many'. serién = serían, 'would be'.

sentences.t: Todas estas ganançias fizo el Canpeador.
sentences.l: All these gains made the Campeador.
sentences.i: All these gains the Campeador had won.
sentences.n: Tirada 122 (assonance ó) — the Çid, at the height of his glory, thinks of mastering Morocco; the Infantes rich and honoured at the Çid's court (Pidal: El Cid, en el colmo de su gloria, medita dominar a Marruecos. — Los infantes ricos y honrados en la corte del Cid). The line-ends run Canpeador, señor, so, onor, Carrión, Criador, pavor, son, noch, yo …: stressed ó again (noch, cut down from noche, and cort count with it). fizo = hizo, f- for h-: fazer ganançias, 'to make gains'. Canpeador with n, as printed.

sentences.t:
“Grado ha Dios que del mundo es señor!
Antes fu minguado, agora rico so,
que he aver e tierra e oro e onor,
e son mios yernos ifantes de Carrión;
sentences.i: “Thanks be to God, who is lord of the world! Once I was in want, and now I am rich: I have wealth and land, gold and lands and lordship, and my sons-in-law are Infantes of Carrión.
sentences.n: Grado ha Dios, ha = a, the preposition with a silent h; the line closes with ! and no ¡, as printed. fu = fui, 'I was'; minguado, 'lacking, in want' (= menguado); so = soy. he, 'I have', present of aver as a full verb, 'to have, hold'; the aver after it is the noun, 'wealth, goods'. Pidal's note to v. 2495: onor puede significar aquí 'heredades', como en 289, o bien 'feudos', como en 887 — 'onor may mean here "landed estates", as in 289, or else "fiefs", as in 887'. ifantes, 'Infantes', sons of a great house. The Çid counts the match among his riches: the marriage still looks to him like a rise in rank.

sentences.t:
arranco las lides commo plaze al Criador,
moros e cristianos de mí han grant pavor.
sentences.l:
I-win the battles as pleases to-the Creator,
Moors and Christians of me have great fear.
sentences.i: I win my battles as it pleases the Creator; Moors and Christians stand in great fear of me.
sentences.n: arranco, 'I win, I rout', arrancar las lides, 'to win the battles'. plaze = place, 'pleases'. pavor, 'fear, dread'; aver pavor de, 'to be afraid of'.

sentences.t:
Allá dentro en Marruecos, o las mezquitas son,
que abrám de mi salto quiçab alguna noch
ellos lo temen, ca non lo pie[n]sso yo:
sentences.l:
There inside in Morocco, where the mosques are,
that they-will-have of my assault perhaps some night
they it fear, for not it think I:
sentences.i: Away over there in Morocco, where the mosques stand, they fear that some night, maybe, they will have me upon them; they fear it, though I have no such thought.
sentences.n: o, 'where' (= donde). abrám = avrán, 'they will have': de mi salto, 'of my assault', a sudden raid by night. quiçab, 'perhaps' (= quizá). noch = noche, the e cut off. Pidal's note to v. 2500: 'Allá en Marruecos temen que quizá yo les asalte cualquier noche' — 'over there in Morocco they fear that perhaps I may fall upon them some night'. The que clause comes before its verb: ellos lo temen picks it up. ca, 'for'; pie[n]sso, 'I think, intend', the n Pidal's: the Çid disclaims the plan in the act of naming it.

sentences.t:
no los iré buscar, en Valençia seré yo,
ellos me darán parias con ayuda del Criador,
que paguen a mí o a qui yo ovier sabor.”
sentences.l:
not them I-will-go to-seek, in Valençia I-will-be I,
they to-me will-give tributes with help of-the Creator,
that they-pay to me or to whom I may-have pleasure.”
sentences.i: I shall not go to seek them out; I shall stay in Valencia, and they will pay me tribute, with the Creator's help, paying it to me or to whomever I please.”
sentences.n: no los iré buscar, the pronoun before ir, 'I will not go seek them'. seré, 'I shall be, remain' (ser of place, where modern Spanish says estar). parias, 'tribute', paid by Moorish rulers to a Christian lord for peace. qui = quien. ovier = oviere, future subjunctive of aver; aver sabor, 'to wish, please' (as at v. 2478). Pidal's note to v. 2504: 'que paguen a mí o a quien yo quisiere' — 'that they pay me or whomever I wish'. This is the rubric's medita dominar a Marruecos: lordship over Morocco by tribute, without a campaign.

sentences.i: Great is the rejoicing in Valencia the great among all the companies of my Çid the Campeador, over this victory they fought with all their heart;
sentences.n: Pidal prints v. 2508 here, before v. 2507, keeping both numbers. In the manuscript d' aquesta arrancada que lidiaron de coraçón comes after the line on the sons-in-law's joy; set here, the hard fighting belongs to the Çid's companies, not to the Infantes. No footnote on the page explains the move; that reading of its effect is ours. [la mayor], 'the great', Valencia's standing epithet, the whole phrase Pidal's restoration; [de], the whole word his. conpañas, 'companies, the men of his household'. sus … [de] mio Çid, the possessive spelled out by the name. aquesta = esta. de coraçón, 'with heart, in earnest'.

sentences.i: great too is the joy of his two sons-in-law: the two of them won the worth of five thousand marks, and many hold the Infantes of Carrión to be rich men.
sentences.n: v. 2507, printed after 2508 (see the note above). s[o]s = sus, the o Pidal's. valía, 'value, worth': the value of five thousand marks, gold or silver by weight. muchos tienen por ricos ifantes de Carrión: 'many hold the Infantes of Carrión (to be) rich', tener por, 'to hold, account', with the Infantes its object, without the personal a. Reading muchos instead as the adverb agreeing in number (as in Muchos son alegres, v. 2473), with the Infantes as subject, 'the Infantes count themselves very rich', would want a se that the line does not have; it is the less likely reading, though not impossible. The rubric's Los infantes ricos y honrados, 'rich and honoured', fits the first.

sentences.i: They came with the others to the court. There with my Çid is the bishop Don Jerome, and the good Álvar Fáñez, a fighting knight, and many others whom the Campeador had raised in his house.
sentences.n: la cort, here the Çid's hall in Valencia. do = don, before a name; Jero[me], the me Pidal's: the bishop, Don Jerome. el bueno de Álbar Fáñez, 'the good Álvar Fáñez', literally 'the good one of', a common turn of praise; Álbar accented, as printed. lidiador, 'fighting, warlike'. crió, 'brought up, reared': criar, to raise a young man in one's household, which made him one's man for life.

sentences.i: When the Infantes of Carrión came in, Minaya welcomed them in my Çid's name: “Come this way, kinsmen; we are worth the more for you.”
sentences.n: recibiólos = recibió + los. por mio Çid, 'on behalf of my Çid', as his deputy. Acá, 'hither, this way'. Pidal's note to v. 2517: cuñado significaba, en general, 'pariente por afinidad'; por esto Minaya llama así a los maridos de sus primas — 'cuñado meant in general "relative by marriage"; that is why Minaya calls the husbands of his cousins so': not 'brothers-in-law' in the modern sense. mas valemos por vos, 'we are worth more through you': the courtesy of the house to the high-born sons-in-law, and its irony for hearers who know what the Infantes did in the battle.

sentences.t:
Assí commo llegaron, pagós el Campeador:
“Evades aquí, yernos, la mi[e] mugier de pro,
e amas la[s] mis fijas, don Elvira e doña Sol;
bien vos abraçen e sírvanvos de coraçón.
sentences.l:
As soon-as they-arrived, was-pleased the Campeador:
“Behold here, sons-in-law, the my wife worthy,
and both the my daughters, don Elvira and doña Sol;
well you may-they-embrace and serve-you with heart.
sentences.i: As soon as they came, the Campeador was glad: “Here, sons-in-law, is my worthy wife, and here are both my daughters, Doña Elvira and Doña Sol: may they embrace you well and serve you with all their heart.
sentences.n: Assí commo, 'as soon as'. pagós = pagó + se, 'was pleased' (pagarse). Pidal's note to v. 2519: 'He aquí', v. 253 — 'here is, behold': Evades aquí, 'behold here'. la mi[e] mugier, article + possessive, mie the feminine form, the e Pidal's; mugier = mujer, 'wife'; de pro, 'worthy, of worth'. amas = ambas, 'both'; la[s], the s his. don Elvira, with don, as printed (doña Sol beside it). abraçen and sírvanvos, present subjunctives of wish; sírvanvos = sírvan + vos. In the manuscript two more lines followed here (vençiemos moros en campo e matamos / a aquel rey Búcar traydor provado); Pidal moves them into Fernando's speech after v. 2530 and keeps their numbers 2522–2523 (see the note there).

sentences.t:
Grado a santa María, madre del nuestro señor Dios!
destos [v]uestros casamientos vos abredes honor.
Buenos mandados irán a tierras de Carrión.”
sentences.l:
Thanks to holy Mary, mother of-the our lord God!
from-these [y]our marriages you will-have honour.
Good tidings will-go to lands of Carrión.”
sentences.i: Thanks be to Holy Mary, mother of our Lord God! From these marriages of yours you will win honour. Good tidings will go to the lands of Carrión.”
sentences.n: The line closes with ! and no ¡, as printed. del nuestro señor Dios, article + possessive. [v]uestros, the v Pidal's. abredes = avredes (habréis), 'you will have', future of aver, the vowel of the infinitive dropped. honor, 'honour', here so spelled (the poem's ondra, kept distinct from onor, 'estate'). tierras de Carrión, the Infantes' home country, in León. The tirada closes as tirada 120 did, on good news going to Carrión.

sentences.i: At these words the Infante Fernando spoke: “Thanks be to the Creator and to you, honoured Çid! We have so much wealth that it cannot be counted.
sentences.n: Tirada 123 (assonance á-o) — the Infantes' vanity; the jests made of them (Pidal: Vanidad de los infantes. — Burlas de que ellos son objeto). The line-ends run Ferran[do], ondrado, contados, lidiado, matamos, provado, saluo, sonrrisando, alcanço, Ferrando …: stressed á, then o. fabló = habló, f- for h-. [ifant], the whole word Pidal's; Ferran[do], the do his. ondrado, 'honoured'. avemos = hemos, aver 'to have' as a full verb; de averes, 'of goods, of wealth'. no son contados, 'are not (to be) counted'.

sentences.t:
por vos avemos ondra e avemos lidiado,
vençiemos moros en campo e matamos
a aquel rey Búcar traydor provado.
sentences.l:
through you we-have honour and we-have fought,
we-conquered Moors in field and we-killed
that king Búcar traitor proven.
sentences.i: Through you we have honour, and we have fought: we beat the Moors in the field and we killed that King Búcar, a proven traitor.
sentences.n: Pidal prints vv. 2522–2523 here, after v. 2530, keeping their numbers: in the manuscript they follow v. 2521, in the Çid's speech to his sons-in-law. His note to v. 2522: matamos a aquel rey Búcar es buena fanfarronada en boca de Fernando, y contrasta con el matastes a Búcar que antes dijo Minaya, v. 2458 — '"we killed that King Búcar" is a fine piece of bragging in Fernando's mouth, and contrasts with the "you killed Búcar" that Minaya said earlier, v. 2458'. (The print sets no label on Minaya's line Matastes a Búcar: counting from its labels 2455 and 2460 it falls at 2457, and the published cid-tiradas-118-119 numbers it so. Pidal's own 2458 is the number it takes if the second label 2455, on “Grado a Dios e al padre…”, is a slip for 2456, as the notes to that part suggest; this footnote supports that reading.) The second moved line is labelled 2553 in the print, plainly a slip for 2523. ondra = honra, 'honour'. avemos lidiado, 'we have fought'. vençiemos = vencimos. matamos … a aquel rey Búcar, the personal a, the object running on into the next line. traydor provado, 'proven traitor', a stock insult for an enemy. Búcar fell to the Çid alone (v. 2425).

sentences.t: Pensad de lo otro, que lo nuestro tenémoslo en saluo.”
sentences.l: Think of the other, for the ours we-hold-it in safety.”
sentences.i: Give your thought to other matters: what is ours we hold in safe keeping.”
sentences.n: Pensad de, 'think of, see to'. Pidal's note to v. 2531: 'cuidaos de otras cosas, que lo nuestro ya está a buen recaudo' — 'take care of other things, for what is ours is already in safe keeping'. tenémoslo, the object said twice, lo nuestro and lo. saluo, with u for v, as printed (= salvo). The Infante tells the Çid what to attend to: the rubric's vanidad.

sentences.i: My Çid's vassals sat there smiling: who had fought best, they asked, or who had gone in the pursuit? But Diego and Fernando they did not find there.
sentences.n: se[d]iense = sedíen + se, 'were sitting', imperfect of seer (= ser, estar, 'to sit, be'), the d Pidal's; the exact extent of his italic here is not certain. sonrrisando, 'smiling'. lidiara, the -ra form as a pluperfect, 'had fought'. f[o]ra = fuera, the -ra pluperfect of ir (which shares these forms with ser), 'had gone', the o his. Pidal's note to v. 2533: 'o quien había ido en la persecución del enemigo' — 'or who had gone in the pursuit of the enemy': alcanço = alcance, 'pursuit'. The line gives the men's talk without a verb of saying. i, 'there', in that reckoning of who fought best. Dí[da]go = Diego, the da Pidal's (the extent of the italic is not certain): the jest is that the Infantes' names never came up.

sentences.t:
Por aquestos juegos que ivan levantando,
elas noches e los días tan mal los escarmentando,
tan mal se conssejaron estos iffantes amos.
sentences.l:
Through these jests that they-were-raising,
the nights and the days so ill them chastising,
so ill themselves counselled these Infantes both.
sentences.i: Because of these jests they kept raising, galling them so cruelly night and day, these two Infantes laid their wicked plan.
sentences.n: juegos, 'jests, mockery'; ivan levantando, ir + gerund, 'kept raising'. Pidal's note to v. 2536: elas noches e los dias, 'siempre, continuamente'; comp. 222 — 'always, continually; compare v. 222'. Pidal quotes elas noches e los dias as one phrase and prints no circumflex (his mark for two words run together, as in ên): elas is most likely the archaic full form of the article (= las), as ela at v. 473, set against los días; e + las, 'and the nights …', is possible (so the note to v. 992 took elas there). Either way the sense is Pidal's 'always'; the form is not certain. escarmentar, 'to chastise, teach a hard lesson', here of the mockery that stung them; the gerund hangs loose, with the vassals as its subject. conssejarse, 'to take counsel': tan mal se conssejaron, 'so evilly did they plot'. iffantes, with ff, as printed. The poet names the motive for what is to come: wounded pride.

sentences.t:
Amos salieron a part, veramientre son hermanos;
desto que ellos fáblaron nos parte non ayamos;
sentences.l:
Both went-out apart, truly they-are brothers;
of-this that they spoke we part not may-have;
sentences.i: The two went off by themselves (true brothers they are); in what they said there may we have no part.
sentences.n: a part, 'aside, apart'. veramientre, 'truly' (= verdaderamente): brothers in deed as in blood. fáblaron, accented as printed (= hablaron). Pidal's note to v. 2539: 'en la maldad que hablaron ellos no tengamos nosotros parte ninguna' — 'in the wickedness they spoke, may we have no part at all'; nos is the singer and his hearers. He adds that D. Hinard cree que aquí empieza el discurso de los infantes, refiriéndose a las bromas de los del Cid — 'Hinard believes the Infantes' speech begins here, referring to the jests of the Çid's men' ('A ces méchants propos ne nous exposons pas davantage', 'let us not expose ourselves further to these spiteful words'), and that Adam traduce bien, 'Adam translates rightly' (presumably as Pidal reads the line). ayamos = hayamos, present subjunctive of aver.

sentences.t:
—“Vayamos pora Carrión, aquí mucho detardamos.
Los averes que tenemos grandes son e sobejanos,
despender no lo[s] podremos mientra que [bivos seamos].
sentences.l:
—“Let-us-go to Carrión, here much we-delay.
The goods that we-have great are and exceeding,
spend not them we-shall-be-able while that [alive we-may-be].
sentences.i: “Let us go to Carrión; we tarry here too long. The wealth we have is great beyond measure; we shall never be able to spend it as long as we live.
sentences.n: The Infantes speak, the two together. The speech opens with a dash and a quotation mark (—“), as Pidal prints it, and runs on into tirada 124: there is no closing quote in this part. Vayamos, 'let us go'; pora = para. detardar, 'to delay, linger'; mucho, 'too long'. sobejanos, 'excessive, overflowing', the word of v. 2482. despender, 'to spend'; lo[s], the s Pidal's. mientra que, 'while, as long as'. [bivos seamos], 'we may be alive', the whole phrase Pidal's restoration, bivo = vivo.
